## 3. AI/ML in Software Engineering Reviews

The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) into software engineering practices is a rapidly evolving field, with recent literature highlighting diverse applications, challenges, and emerging methodologies. A significant trend involves the application of Large Language Models (LLMs) across various stages of the software development lifecycle. For instance, LLMs are being rigorously evaluated for their code generation capabilities, with new benchmarks like RealisticCodeBench introduced to assess their performance on practical coding tasks from GitHub repositories [371]. This extends to specialized domains, such as the generation of Verilog code, where LLMs are seen as a critical research area at the intersection of Software Engineering (SE) and AI [369]. However, a notable limitation in this area is the persistent challenge of "hallucinations" in code generation LLMs, necessitating ongoing research into their taxonomy, benchmarks, and mitigation strategies [187].

Beyond code generation, AI methods are increasingly employed in requirements engineering (RE). A systematic mapping study explores recent changes in the use of personas in RE, specifically noting the evolution of Generative AI approaches to represent user expectations and needs [241]. Furthermore, AI methods are being systematically reviewed for their role in the quality assessment of software requirements [363]. To address data scarcity in critical domains, natural language processing (NLP) and data augmentation techniques are being explored to enhance natural language software requirements [177]. AI also shows promise in automating web accessibility remediation by leveraging LLMs to generate inherently accessible content, as proposed by a conceptual model [353].

In software quality assurance and testing, AI-powered methods are gaining traction. A systematic literature review highlights the role of AI in developing automated and remote User Experience (UX) evaluation methods, analyzing 55 peer-reviewed articles from 2014 to 2024 [197]. Similarly, automation and AI are being investigated for their potential in usability issue detection, aiming to overcome the cost and time-consuming nature of traditional techniques [180]. For security, automated vulnerability repair, often leveraging AI, is a critical area given the increasing complexity of software and the labor-intensive nature of manual fixes [154]. Deep neural models are also surveyed for their application in coverage-guided greybox fuzzing, a technique for software testing [274].

The broader implications of AI in software engineering extend to process improvement and ethical considerations. AI is being integrated with process mining to design, sustain, and improve collaborative processes, especially in increasingly complex organizational environments [290]. The concept of "Human-Machine Teaming" (HMT) is emerging, viewing AI tools for SE (AI4SE) as team members rather than mere instruments, which may enhance team effectiveness [283]. Furthermore, the responsible development of AI systems is underscored by research into strategic motivators for ethical AI, emphasizing the need for planning, governance, and understanding key drivers [11].

Addressing challenges inherent in AI/ML development itself, Artificial Intelligence Bills of Materials (AIBOMs) have emerged as structured artifacts to document AI supply chain components, aiming to improve transparency, accountability, and security [255]. Technical debt is a significant concern in AI/ML applications, particularly within competition platforms, due to rapid experimentation and complex data pipelines [320]. To mitigate insufficient data volume and quality, AI simulation using virtual training environments and synthetic data generated by digital twins is proposed for safer and more efficient AI agent development [9e0c9feb-7193-4f50-b4ba-f463af3a21ba]. Visualization tools for Machine Learning pipelines are also reviewed to address the increasing complexity and adoption of ML pipelines [132].

Overall, a clear pattern is the pervasive application of AI/ML to automate, enhance, and evaluate various software engineering tasks, from requirements to testing and maintenance. However, many papers highlight that the field is still in its early stages, with ongoing efforts to establish robust evaluation benchmarks [371], address inherent limitations like AI hallucinations [187], and develop structured guidance for ethical and transparent AI system development [11]. The reliance on systematic reviews and surveys within these papers also indicates a current focus on consolidating existing knowledge and identifying future research agendas.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) methodologies is increasingly prevalent across various facets of software engineering, ranging from foundational architectural design to advanced review processes. A significant trend involves leveraging AI, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), to automate and enhance traditional software development tasks. For instance, AI is envisioned to address longstanding challenges in software architecture design and evolution [68], while a functional software reference architecture has been proposed to guide the integration of LLMs into software systems [69].

In the realm of software quality and analysis, ML techniques are applied for data preprocessing in code smell detection [298] and for static source code analysis using graph machine learning [210]. ML also contributes to code summarization and comprehension, aiming to improve developer understanding and maintenance efficiency [212]. Furthermore, AI-based approaches are explored for requirements prioritization, offering a more efficient alternative to manual, time-consuming methods [206]. LLMs are specifically being investigated for assisting requirements engineering in agile model-driven development, though empirical guidance for their industrial application remains limited [324]. Beyond these, ML techniques are being studied to enhance software team effort estimations [315], and AI-assisted knowledge graph approaches are evaluated for software package selection in open-source ecosystems [110]. The methodological integration of LLMs into Mining Software Repositories (MSR) is also an emerging area, though currently poorly understood [217].

A notable pattern is the application of AI, particularly LLMs, to automate and streamline the systematic literature review (SLR) process itself. LLMs are being surveyed for their potential in automated scholarly paper review [384] and leveraged for semi-automatic corpus filtration, addressing the time-consuming manual effort involved [161]. Tools like ProfOlaf are being developed to provide semi-automated support for SLRs, aiming to reduce labor intensity and error rates [3].

The engineering of AI/ML systems introduces unique challenges. Non-functional requirements (NFRs) in ML-enabled systems present a distinct set of classification and implementation challenges [216]. Requirements engineering for ML-based AI systems is a critical area, with secondary literature highlighting various development challenges [218]. Misuses of ML cloud services are also a concern, necessitating a comprehensive understanding of potential vulnerabilities [f955291e-a77e-48d2-b095-cf06f4987f1c]. A significant limitation identified is the critical bottleneck in evaluating the massive volume of software artifacts generated by LLMs, leading to the concept of "LLM-as-a-Judge" to address this scalability issue [149]. Furthermore, in software traceability link recovery between natural language and programming language artifacts, relying solely on textual similarity is insufficient due to the semantic gap, indicating a need for more advanced AI/ML techniques [387].

AI/ML also plays a crucial role in enhancing security and reliability. Adaptive decision trees with random forest integration are proposed for efficient botnet forensics [35]. ML-based Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS) are critical for IoT security, although their effectiveness is challenged by the complexity of IoT environments and the quality of benchmark datasets [40]. Federated and explainable ML approaches are being developed for secure and trustworthy Social Internet of Things (SIoT) applications [325]. The demand for transparent AI models has led to surveys on Explainable AI (XAI) for internet traffic classification, prediction, and intrusion detection [247]. Additionally, AI-driven personalized privacy assistants are being researched to aid users in privacy-related decision-making [231]. Beyond software engineering, ML is applied in broader contexts such as detecting anomalous vessel trajectories using collaborative clustering [285] and for sustainable reconstruction planning after natural disasters [236].

The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) methodologies is profoundly reshaping various facets of software engineering, driven by advancements in data-driven methods and large language models (LLMs). Systematic literature reviews and surveys highlight the growing interest and application of these technologies across the software development lifecycle, from initial requirements to post-deployment maintenance and evaluation.

A significant trend is the application of LLMs in diverse software engineering tasks. For instance, LLMs are being systematically surveyed for their utility in static code analysis, where they show promise in detecting vulnerabilities, errors, and programming issues without code execution [296]. In requirements engineering (RE), LLM agents are widely used, with ongoing research focused on enhancing their accuracy through prompt engineering, model fine-tuning, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) [262]. Multi-agent debate strategies are also being explored to further improve RE tasks with LLMs [262]. The effectiveness of specific LLMs, such as ChatGPT, in secure code development, including autonomous code generation and analysis, is also under assessment [66]. Beyond code, LLMs are empirically studied for their ability to augment UML class diagrams by generating behavioral methods from natural language use cases [289]. The "LLM-as-a-judge" paradigm is emerging as a promising approach for automated evaluation, aiming to align with multi-dimensional human evaluation in NLP applications [81].

Beyond LLMs, ML pipelines are recognized for addressing challenges in ensuring quality and efficiency across the entire software engineering lifecycle, especially as systems grow in complexity [169]. AI-led design innovation is a burgeoning field, necessitating a deeper understanding of design-centric AI methods and the types of assistance they provide [188]. In software maintenance, deep learning techniques are increasingly integrated with information retrieval-based bug localization to expedite the identification of buggy code [254], complementing research in ticket-level bug prediction to optimize testing efforts [272]. AI's role extends to web testing, where it is driving new methodologies and tools [172], and in automated and remote user experience (UX) evaluation, synthesizing insights on key AI technologies and their applications [199]. The concept of "Vibe Coding" further illustrates the trend of human-AI co-creation, blending AI-assisted tooling with developer intuition [53].

Despite these advancements, several challenges and limitations persist. Maintainability and scalability are critical concerns for ML systems, requiring robust solutions as applications become more complex and widespread [313][314]. The "black-box" nature of many AI systems necessitates the development of Explanation User Interfaces (XUI) to make their decision-making processes intelligible to users and developers [73]. The rapid proliferation of intelligent systems technologies, including AI and ML, also intensifies big data governance challenges for organizations [55]. Furthermore, the nascent stage of Generative AI application in software architecture means systematic understanding of its use, rationale, and contexts is still developing [105]. There is also a recognized need to assess and advance benchmarks for effectively evaluating LLMs in various software engineering tasks [155]. The human-AI experience in integrated development environments (IDEs) is a critical area, with research exploring how AI integration fundamentally alters developer interaction with tools [310]. Finally, broader discussions emphasize the deep connection between AI safety and potential existential risks, urging serious consideration of these threats in AI development [138].
## 4. Systematic Reviews of AI/ML in Software

The landscape of software engineering is increasingly shaped by the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML), leading to a growing body of systematic literature reviews (SLRs) that explore this intersection. These reviews span various stages of the software development lifecycle, address critical system properties, and examine the impact of emerging AI technologies.

A significant focus is on leveraging AI/ML to enhance software engineering processes. Large Language Models (LLMs) are being explored for automating literature research and review generation, aiming to overcome information overload [dec6480a-2380-4fe9-9e5e-4adf3525ad22]. Similarly, active learning, an ML technique, is applied to improve the efficiency of screening records in systematic reviews and meta-analyses [63]. Within the development phase, ML techniques are systematically mapped for their application in requirement engineering activities [146] and for automatic user story generation [300]. AI methods are also reviewed for their role in software refactoring to improve code quality [233]. In testing and quality assurance, learning-based approaches are investigated for continuous integration [41], and the intersection of testing with Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a subject of structured review [250]. Furthermore, Deep Learning (DL) is being applied to code smell detection, with a specific focus on data preparation challenges [379]. The operationalization of ML models in software is captured by analyses of MLOps architectures [245].

Beyond process improvements, AI/ML is critically examined for its impact on software system properties like security and reliability. Reviews highlight the security implications of code generated by LLMs [282][251] and the use of LLMs for vulnerability detection and repair [383]. Adversarial Machine Learning (AML) attacks and defenses in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) are surveyed [326], alongside taxonomies of system-level attacks on Deep Learning models in autonomous vehicles [334]. Anomaly detection, often ML-driven, is a recurring theme, applied to log analysis in software systems [209], adaptive detection for cyber-physical systems [232], and IoT botnet DDoS attacks [126][224].

The emergence of advanced AI paradigms also garners significant review attention. Digital Twin technology, often intertwined with AI simulation, is surveyed for its state-of-the-art, reference frameworks [198], and the role of multi-agents [167], including its network landscape, privacy, and security [295]. Generative AI models raise concerns about intellectual property protection for training data [302], while LLM-based multi-agent systems are envisioned for future software engineering applications [148]. Other applications include ML techniques for financial fraud detection [43], explainable biometrics [340], and facial recognition payment systems [372].

A notable pattern across these reviews is the prevalence of systematic literature reviews, mapping studies, and surveys as primary methodologies, reflecting a collective effort to consolidate knowledge in a rapidly evolving field. Many contributions involve proposing taxonomies, frameworks, or identifying research gaps, such as the analysis of MLOps architectures [245] or the technical risk model for ML-based software projects [196]. The increasing adoption of AI for resilience in supply chains is also explored [359].

Despite the breadth of coverage, several limitations emerge. Many reviews highlight the nascent stage of research in certain areas, such as the security of LLM-generated code [282][251] or the application of ML in specific software engineering activities like requirement engineering [146]. The rapid evolution of AI/ML technologies means that reviews can quickly become outdated, necessitating continuous updates. Furthermore, while many reviews identify challenges and future directions, empirical validation of proposed AI/ML solutions in real-world software development contexts often remains limited, as noted in the context of MLOps [245]. The focus on identifying existing literature also means that these reviews often reflect the state of published research rather than current industrial practice, which may be more advanced or face different challenges.

The intersection of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) with software engineering practices is a rapidly evolving field, as evidenced by a substantial body of recent systematic reviews and surveys. These reviews collectively highlight the diverse applications of AI/ML in various stages of the software lifecycle, alongside critical challenges and emerging research directions.

A prominent area of focus is the application of AI/ML to enhance software quality and maintenance. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), for instance, have been systematically reviewed for their utility in code clone research, aiming to mitigate negative effects on software quality and maintenance [276]. Similarly, supervised learning models are extensively surveyed for their role in detecting code smells, which are indicators of potential design problems [380]. The forecasting and prediction of technical debt evolution, crucial for informed software maintenance, also leverage AI/ML techniques, as explored in a dedicated systematic literature review [10]. Beyond code analysis, Multi-Label Learning (MLL) has seen increasing application in software engineering (MLL4SE), addressing problems where multiple labels are associated with a single instance [157]. Furthermore, the integration of Machine Learning into Model-Driven Engineering (MDE) paradigms is a growing trend, with a systematic review mapping its current state and future potential [213].

Requirements engineering (RE) is another domain significantly impacted by AI. A systematic mapping study investigates the application of AI techniques for requirements classification, a challenging aspect of RE [171]. However, the development of AI-based systems introduces new complexities for RE, including difficulties in specifying and validating requirements and considering ethical implications, which are explored in another systematic mapping study [140]. The broader application of AI to formal methods, aiming to provide sound and verifiable reasoning in computer science, also constitutes a significant research trend [327].

A critical cross-cutting theme is the explainability of AI (XAI), particularly for ML/DL-based software engineering research. The "black-box" nature of many AI algorithms necessitates research into explainability to foster trust and facilitate adoption [72]. This concern extends to the broader field of XAI, with tertiary reviews synthesizing the landscape of existing methods and identifying trends towards more interactive AI systems [234][278]. Human-AI interaction is also explored in the context of AI assistance for UX practitioners, though mainstream adoption of such tools remains limited [204]. The evaluation of user experience (UX) for AI systems, such as chatbots, even extends to physiological measures like electroencephalography (EEG) [112].

Security is another vital area where AI/ML plays a dual role: as a tool for enhancing security and as a source of new vulnerabilities. AI/ML techniques are applied to tasks like identifying authorship in malicious binaries [40807083-4c8b-4f9-b94f-42d1478f292a] and automating penetration testing through path planning [82]. Conversely, the security of AI systems themselves is a growing concern, with surveys addressing adversarial machine learning for code data [370], failure analysis and fault injection in AI systems [374], and the complex risks associated with the Large Language Model (LLM) supply chain [156]. The advent of LLMs has also prompted systematic investigations into prompting techniques for secure code generation, highlighting both potential and challenges [336].

The operationalization of ML models in production environments, known as MLOps, is a critical area, with a multivocal review synthesizing practices, challenges, and open issues, such as integrating ML models with non-ML software and continuous monitoring [99]. Reinforcement learning (RL) has also found application in optimizing processes like Technology Assisted Review (TAR) by developing novel stopping rules [61].

A common methodology across these papers is the systematic literature review (SLR) or systematic mapping study (SMS), indicating a commitment to rigorous and transparent synthesis of existing research. However, a notable limitation across many of these reviews is the inherent challenge of keeping pace with the rapid advancements in AI/ML, particularly with emerging technologies like LLMs. Many abstracts highlight gaps in current research, such as the limited mainstream adoption of AI-enabled tools [204] or the need for more comprehensive approaches to address the black-box nature of AI [72]. The reliance on abstract excerpts for analysis, due to the provided data format, may also limit the depth of understanding regarding specific methodological details or nuanced findings within each review.

The landscape of AI/ML in software engineering is characterized by a multifaceted approach, encompassing foundational data management, complex system architectures, operational challenges, and critical ethical considerations. A significant portion of recent literature employs systematic review methodologies to synthesize existing knowledge and identify future research directions.

Several systematic literature reviews (SLRs) highlight the critical role of data and its management in AI/ML systems. One SLR explores factors impacting the adoption of big data in healthcare, noting its potential to improve patient health and operational efficiency [401410bd-0b84-4a1c-a26f-1aca11a4f4a]. Complementing this, a mapping study specifically addresses data engineering for AI systems, revealing that despite the maturity of AI models, organizations frequently struggle with the necessary data infrastructure [150]. This underscores data as a fundamental component and a significant bottleneck in AI system development and deployment.

Beyond data, the engineering of complex software systems that often integrate AI/ML components is a prominent theme. A review of digital assistants (DAs) in production and logistics identifies their applications, benefits, and challenges across information management, collaborative operations, and knowledge transfer, implicitly relying on AI/ML capabilities [382]. In the realm of robotics, an SLR on commonsense knowledge in cognitive robotics emphasizes its necessity for generalization in unknown tasks and environments, highlighting a core challenge for advanced AI applications [343]. Furthermore, the evolution of software engineering for Systems-of-Systems (SoS) is explored, noting the increased connectivity and integration that lead to emergent behaviors in modern systems [77]. The complexity of such systems is further addressed by a comparison study of static analysis architecture recovery tools for microservice applications, which are crucial for understanding the structure of distributed software systems [305].

Operationalizing and measuring the success of software development practices, particularly those supporting AI/ML, also receives attention. A multivocal literature review on DevOps metrics and KPIs reveals the ongoing difficulty organizations face in effectively measuring DevOps success, despite widespread implementation efforts [38]. This highlights a gap in understanding how to quantify the impact of agile and continuous delivery practices on AI/ML projects. Moreover, the human element in software development is acknowledged through a secondary study on social and cultural factors influencing software requirements prioritization, emphasizing the highly social nature of this critical process [80].

Finally, ethical and responsible development practices are gaining prominence. A critical literature review on Responsible Design Thinking for Sustainable Development proposes a new conceptual framework and research agenda, underscoring the importance of ethical considerations in design processes, a principle increasingly vital for AI/ML systems [49].

A notable pattern across these papers is the prevalence of systematic review methodologies, including SLRs [401410bd-0b84-4a1c-a26f-1aca11a4f4a, 3d04b7f4-ec46-471b-9b62-3d3b242766fa, d73d084e-892c-41bf-b743-85e9849149e3], multivocal reviews [38], mapping studies [150], and critical reviews [49]. This indicates a strong academic focus on synthesizing existing knowledge to understand complex and evolving domains related to AI/ML in software. The notable results emphasize that data infrastructure [150], architectural complexity [77][305], and the integration of human-centric factors, including ethics and commonsense [80][343][49], are central challenges in modern software development, particularly for AI/ML systems.

Limitations specific to these papers often stem from their nature as reviews or secondary studies. While providing valuable syntheses, they inherently rely on the quality and scope of the primary literature they analyze, which may introduce biases or gaps not explicitly addressed in their abstracts. For instance, the mapping study on data engineering for AI systems identifies organizational struggles but does not offer new empirical solutions [150]. Similarly, the critical literature review on Responsible Design Thinking proposes a framework and agenda, which, by definition, requires further empirical validation [49]. The comparison study of architecture recovery tools is limited to specific tools and microservice contexts [305], potentially limiting the generalizability of its findings to other architectural styles or toolsets. Furthermore, the domain-specific focus of some reviews, such as big data in healthcare [401410bd-0b84-4a1c-a26f-1aca11a4f4a] or digital assistants in production and logistics [382], means their specific findings may not be directly transferable to all AI/ML software contexts, though the underlying challenges often resonate across domains.
## 5. Systematic Reviews of Security Topics

The thematic area of "Systematic Reviews of Security Topics" reveals a dynamic research landscape, heavily influenced by the rapid evolution of digital technologies. This section synthesizes findings from various systematic literature reviews, mapping studies, and surveys that address critical security concerns across diverse domains.

A substantial portion of the literature focuses on the security of emerging technologies, particularly the Internet of Things (IoT). Reviews have meticulously documented exploitation techniques for IoST vulnerabilities in air-gapped networks, outlining essential security measures [143]. Trust management in IoT systems is a recurring theme, with surveys exploring methods to ensure reliability in potentially hostile environments [176]. The integration of Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) for enhancing IoT security, including defense against spoofing, Denial of Service (DoS) attacks, and malware, has been systematically reviewed [23]. Furthermore, the application of blockchain technology to IoT forensic investigation models has been examined, highlighting its potential for secure evidence management [12]. Privacy concerns in IoT systems, specifically how artificial intelligence can be leveraged to address them, also form a key area of systematic inquiry [129]. Model-based security testing is presented as a structured approach to identify vulnerabilities in IoT systems [202].

Artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) feature prominently, both as tools for enhancing security and as systems requiring their own security considerations. Systematic mapping studies have charted the landscape of deep learning techniques employed for detecting cybersecurity attacks [337]. Conversely, ensuring the safety and reliability of AI systems is critical, with mapping studies exploring techniques like Fault Tree Analysis (FTA) and Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (FMECA) for AI-integrated systems [215]. The broader implications of human-AI interaction in safety-critical industries, where system failures can have severe consequences, have been reviewed, emphasizing the need for robust interaction design [9cdd5bcf-becd-42c2-800b

The body of literature extensively employs systematic literature reviews (SLRs) and systematic mapping studies (SMS) to synthesize knowledge across various security domains, reflecting a common methodological approach to consolidate fragmented research [173], [16], [56]. These reviews often highlight the nascent or scattered nature of research in their respective fields, underscoring the need for comprehensive overviews [16], [56], [191].

A significant portion of the reviewed literature focuses on privacy and data protection. Research explores the automated analysis of privacy policies, identifying it as a multidisciplinary field with a growing but scattered knowledge base [16]. Other studies delve into managing privacy in B2B marketing, noting the detrimental consequences of poor information privacy for businesses [152]. Understanding online privacy is advanced through reviews of privacy visualizations and Privacy by Design guidelines [51]. Data anonymization techniques for pervasive healthcare are also systematically mapped, addressing challenges in data privacy, transparency, and trustworthiness within digital health [388]. The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is a recurring theme, with analyses of ontologies and policy languages capable of representing its rights and obligations [106], and a study on privacy patterns research [190].

Cybersecurity threats and defensive mechanisms are another prominent area. Reviews cover Host-based Intrusion Detection Systems (HIDS) utilizing Natural Language Processing (NLP) methods [330] and those inspired by Swarm Intelligence [248]. The increasing rate of cybercrimes is examined through the lens of Routine Activity Theory [669ddfb9-21ea-411c-a46a-81f3a6ebe61a]. Machine learning (ML) is frequently explored for detection purposes, including Android mobile malware [308] and sophisticated data exfiltration attacks [291]. The use of security logs for data leak detection is also systematically reviewed [389]. Furthermore, the evolution, incentives, and detection of botnets are surveyed [5feaad8c-d30c-44ca-bcaf-e1846b4f75a3], and the role of recommender systems in cybersecurity is discussed [268].

Human factors in security are critically examined, with phishing attacks being a key focus due to users' vulnerabilities and difficulties in risk comprehension [94]. The challenges developers face in programming securely are highlighted, alongside reviews of methods for user studies with developers and systematizations of security API usability recommendations [83], [266]. The complex and multifaceted meaning of "usable security" is also explored [191], and the memorability of different password creation strategies is evaluated [192].

Security in advanced architectures and emerging technologies forms another significant cluster. Blockchain technology is reviewed for its application in access control mechanisms [52], Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI) models [303], securing the Internet and IoT [201], and identity management systems in Health IoT [17]. The financial services sector's adoption of blockchain is also analyzed [25], alongside the broader digital money revolution from cryptocurrencies to Central Bank Digital Currencies [91]. Microservice security is a growing concern, with dedicated systematic reviews [56], [348]. The convergence of cloud computing and IoT necessitates reviews of software architectures [50], while security and privacy concerns in connected cars are systematically mapped [281]. Cyber resilience and incident response in smart cities are also critical areas of investigation [9]. Cloud adoption in e-government [2], cloud management and monitoring [258], and Quality of Service (QoS) in industrial cloud environments [183] are also addressed, where security is an implicit or explicit concern.

Information security risk management (ISRM) in IT outsourcing is identified as a critical yet under-studied area [59]. The quality dimensions of threat intelligence for research and practice are also explored [385], alongside a mapping of security standards to understand compliance requirements [240]. Information sharing in cybersecurity is reviewed, categorizing papers by focus and methodological approaches [265]. Architectural tactics for Big Data Cybersecurity Analytic Systems are also reviewed, aiming to protect networks and data from unauthorized access [344].

A notable limitation across many of these systematic reviews is the consistent observation that research in their respective domains remains scattered, lacking a well-defined corpus [16], [56]. This fragmentation often leads to identified gaps in knowledge, inconsistent findings, and a call for more structured future research [669ddfb9-21ea-411c-a46a-81f3a6ebe61a], [191]. For instance, the applicability of Routine Activity Theory in cybercrimes shows inconsistent findings [669ddfb9-21ea-411c-a46a-81f3a6ebe61a], and the literature on microservice security is spread across many venues [56]. The reliance on systematic methodologies itself often serves to address this very limitation, by attempting to bring coherence to diverse bodies of work.

The landscape of cybersecurity research is extensively mapped through systematic reviews, addressing a broad spectrum of technological domains and threats. Reviews frequently employ systematic literature reviews (SLRs) and systematic mapping studies (SMSs) to synthesize existing knowledge and identify research gaps.

A significant body of work focuses on the security of emerging and interconnected systems. Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) and the Internet of Things (IoT) are prominent, with studies exploring their security challenges [205], patterns and architectures for IoT security [280], and specific defense mechanisms like Moving Target Defense (MTD) for IoT [249]. The need for smarter security orchestration and automated response (SOAR) for CPS and IoT is also highlighted, noting gaps in existing approaches [253]. Edge computing, often integral to IoT deployments, faces its own security challenges and requires threat protection strategies [165].

Blockchain technology and smart contracts represent another critical area. Reviews cover smart contract security vulnerabilities and solutions [358], the broader cybersecurity aspects of blockchain [333], and the security challenges arising from cross-chain smart contract invocations [108]. The governance of blockchain, crucial for its safe and appropriate use, is also a subject of systematic review [200], as are cybersecurity challenges in blockchain-based supply chain management systems [147].

Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) introduce unique security considerations. Reviews address adversarial machine learning (AML) attacks and defenses in multi-agent reinforcement learning [5965c5fb-273d-4bbe-a9d8-548c63d84950], the application of deep learning for phishing detection [76], and the security challenges associated with Robotic Process Automation (RPA), AI, and Blockchain in the context of the Fourth Industrial Revolution [15]. The importance of provenance documentation for explainable and trustworthy AI is also explored [166], alongside approaches for AI-supported security risk assessment [103] and the governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) for AI [184].

Beyond specific technologies, reviews examine foundational security practices and management. This includes authentication and authorization in microservices architecture [28], security concepts for configurable data storages [221], and the usability of security Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) [267]. Software security management in critical infrastructures is a vital concern, with reviews identifying key challenges [100]. Cybersecurity metrics for Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs) are also reviewed to help assess their security posture [139], alongside a systematic mapping study on cyber security indicator data [222]. Cloud security, trust, and privacy are collectively mapped, emphasizing their interconnectedness [259].

Privacy, a closely related domain, is also a focus. Reviews investigate privacy nudges for personal information disclosure, noting divergent empirical results [158]. The challenges of contact tracing apps, particularly concerning privacy in neo-liberal societies, are systematically reviewed [13]. Healthcare data security in wireless body area networks (WBANs) is surveyed, highlighting the need for robust protection in this sensitive domain [160].

A common pattern across these reviews is the identification of evolving threats and the necessity for specialized security solutions tailored to specific technological contexts, from the tight cyber-physical coupling of CPS [205] to the decentralized nature of blockchain [333]. Many studies conclude by outlining future research directions, underscoring the dynamic nature of security challenges. Limitations specific to these papers often include the inherent scope constraints of systematic reviews, reliance on published academic literature which may not capture all industry practices, and the rapid pace of technological change which can quickly render some findings partially outdated. For instance, the review on SOAR for IoT/CPS explicitly aims to find gaps in existing approaches [253], indicating that current solutions are insufficient. Similarly, the divergent empirical results on privacy nudges [158] suggest a lack of consistent understanding or effectiveness. The challenge of applying security indicators due to a lack of available or standardized data [222] points to a practical limitation in implementing security measures. The poor usability of security APIs [267] further illustrates practical and design-related limitations identified within the reviewed literature, hindering secure software development. The varying quality and depth of primary studies included in these reviews also present a limitation, impacting the comprehensiveness of the synthesis.

The systematic literature reviews and mapping studies in this collection highlight critical security challenges and advancements across various technological domains, employing rigorous methodologies to synthesize existing knowledge. A significant focus is placed on the security of emerging and complex systems, particularly the Internet of Things (IoT) and Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS). For instance, one systematic literature review investigates model-driven security engineering for cyber-physical systems, noting their increased importance and vulnerability to attackers compared to traditional software products [125]. Similarly, the security analysis of IoT devices, often operating in diverse environments and transmitting large volumes of data, is explored through a systematic literature review leveraging mobile computing [193]. The complexity of designing security and privacy requirements for IoT applications, which integrate both hardware and software across varied nodes, is also a key finding from a survey in this area [22]. Furthermore, another systematic literature review specifically addresses methods for enforcing security within IoT frameworks, recognizing the need for novel approaches in large-scale sensor-based systems [34].

Beyond IoT and CPS, other reviews delve into security mechanisms for distributed and data-intensive architectures. A systematic mapping study identifies security mechanisms pertinent to microservices-based systems, acknowledging the architectural style's advantages but also its inherent security challenges [349]. The protection of confidential data is a central theme in a multivocal literature review on consensus mechanisms in Distributed Ledger Technologies (DLT), which highlights DLT's potential for decentralization and data sovereignty [350]. Relatedly, a systematic literature review on Blockchain-enabled information sharing in supply chains implicitly touches upon security by discussing how this technology can address fragmentation and enhance trust in complex stakeholder networks [ee6f3a15-0efb-400d-9afa-2cdc935b4275]. The architectural considerations for Big Data Cybersecurity Analytics (BDCA) systems are also examined, focusing on leveraging big data technologies to analyze security events and protect organizational assets [345].

Several papers, while not exclusively security-focused, underscore the importance of security and privacy in related domains. A literature review on health data integration, for instance, emphasizes the collaborative utilization of data across systems to provide a comprehensive patient view, inherently requiring robust privacy safeguards [133c8136-9922-4bb0-a5b5-382b94734b]. Similarly, a systematic review evaluating factors influencing cloud technology adoption in health and non-health sectors implicitly acknowledges security as a critical concern for adoption, given the benefits cloud technology offers [293].

A notable pattern across these reviews is the frequent application of systematic literature reviews (SLR) and systematic mapping studies (SMS) to understand complex and rapidly evolving technological landscapes. These methodologies are used to synthesize knowledge on topics ranging from embodied interaction [189] and energy efficiency in robotics software [329] to QoS-aware cloud service composition [311] and IoT interoperability [238][351]. This demonstrates the versatility of these review methods in structuring and understanding diverse research areas.

Limitations identified within these papers often relate to the immaturity or complexity of the reviewed domains. For example, the novelty of Distributed Ledger Technologies means that the fundamentals for their design and development are still emerging, limiting practical implementations and comprehensive understanding [350]. The intricate nature of IoT applications, requiring seamless interaction between software and hardware across varied capabilities, presents significant challenges in designing effective security and privacy requirements [22]. Furthermore, the lack of well-established development guidelines for large-scale machine learning systems in industrial settings points to a broader challenge in managing and securing rapidly advancing technologies [207]. The collection itself, while diverse, illustrates the application of systematic review methodologies across a wide range of topics, some of which only indirectly relate to security.
## 6. Systematic Mapping Studies in Software Engineering

Systematic mapping studies (SMS) and related systematic literature reviews (SLRs) are fundamental methodologies in software engineering research, serving to synthesize existing knowledge, identify research gaps, and map the state-of-the-art across diverse domains. The prevalence of these methods is evident in recent literature, covering a broad spectrum of topics from technical debt to emerging applications of artificial intelligence.

A prominent area of investigation is **technical debt (TD)**, where SMSs have focused on its quantification and management. Studies have explored approaches to quantify TD, often based on identifying "smells," and have developed conceptual models to facilitate understanding [269][270]. The automation of TD management, including the use of intelligent techniques, has also been mapped to identify current practices and future perspectives [60][18]. Beyond TD, **code quality and refactoring** are frequently mapped, with reviews examining code smell datasets and validation mechanisms [377], co-occurrences of code smells [252], and Android-specific smells [365]. The intent behind specific refactorings like "Extract Method" has been systematically reviewed [31], and the application of deep learning to code refactoring has been surveyed [244].

**Software testing** is another extensively mapped domain. SMSs and SLRs have explored the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in testing [36], automated GUI testing over decades [347], and specific techniques like pattern-based [178] and vision-based mobile GUI testing [373]. Model-based testing approaches, including the transformation of abstract tests into code [111] and the use of Coloured Petri nets for test generation [321], have been synthesized. The landscape of automated driving system testing has also been surveyed to identify trends [331].

The intersection of **Machine Learning (ML) and Software Engineering (SE)** is a rapidly growing area for mapping studies. Reviews have charted ML methodologies for requirements management [368], ML-based approaches for continuous integration [42], and the application of ML and deep learning in software defect prediction [328][376]. Furthermore, quality models specifically for AI systems, software, and components have been systematically mapped [24].

**Software architecture and design** are frequently analyzed through mapping studies. These include architectural tactics [242], architectural support for performance in continuous SE [102], and the evaluation of Systems-of-Systems architectures [301]. Microservices architecture, in particular, has seen mapping efforts on Domain-Driven Design applications [297] and the cataloging of anti-patterns and bad smells [78].

Beyond these technical domains, SMSs also address **human and process aspects** of software engineering. This includes the evolution of teamwork quality instruments in Agile development [299], documentation practices in Agile [159], and the benefits and challenges of Behavior-Driven Development [44]. The role of bots in software development has been systematically reviewed [225], as have secondary studies on human aspects in SE [386] and the phenomenon of burnout in software engineering [341].

A common pattern across these mapping studies is the identification of research gaps and future directions. Many reviews explicitly aim to classify existing approaches, tools, or techniques, such as those for software merging [74], vulnerability prediction metrics [86], or memory leak detection [307]. Several studies also focus on mapping the evolution of a field, such as code comprehension experiments over 40 years [366] or the development of GraphQL [275].

A notable limitation observed across many of these mapping studies is the reliance on published academic literature, potentially overlooking insights from grey literature or industry practices that are not formally published. While some studies explicitly include grey literature [354], this is not universal. The scope of these reviews, while broad for their specific topics, is inherently constrained by the chosen search strategies and inclusion criteria, which may limit the comprehensiveness of the mapped landscape. Furthermore, the abstracts provided often lack explicit details on the specific limitations identified by the authors of the primary studies, making it challenging to synthesize common methodological weaknesses beyond the scope of the review itself.

The provided literature, predominantly comprising systematic mapping studies (SMS), systematic literature reviews (SLR), and surveys, highlights the breadth and depth of research in software engineering (SE) [137][335][127][48]. These reviews collectively synthesize existing knowledge, identify research gaps, and characterize various facets of SE practices and technologies.

A significant portion of the literature focuses on **software testing and quality assurance**. Reviews explore testing for context-aware software systems [220][319], Big Data systems [45], and web applications, particularly concerning security [46][284]. The challenges of static analysis alarm postprocessing are also examined [239]. Specific techniques like model-based test case generation and prioritization [230], vertical test reuse for embedded systems [114], and test case prioritization in Continuous Integration environments [195] are systematically mapped. The increasing adoption of software testing in Internet of Things (IoT) applications is also a notable area of review [88]. Beyond testing, broader software quality measurement research is synthesized [79], along with robustness assessment [182] and the qualities of quality itself [79].

Another prominent theme is the **integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) into software engineering**. Several studies investigate the application of computer vision to improve SE tasks [48], data-driven vulnerability assessment and prioritization [185], and deep learning-based vulnerability analysis on source code [306]. The unique challenges of ensuring software quality for AI-based software [127] and testing ML-based systems [286] are explored. Furthermore, the broader engineering perspective on ML systems, including state of the art and challenges, is a recurring focus [130][246]. Technical debt and antipatterns in AI-based systems are also characterized [64].

**Agile, DevOps, and Continuous Software Development (CSD)** methodologies are extensively reviewed. Studies cover user experience practices in software startups [137], documentation challenges in CSD [335], and data-driven effort estimation for agile user stories [33]. The measurement of quality in agile and rapid software development is mapped [208], alongside the integration of explicit risk management into agile methods [c5070d78-0cdf-428d-b9e9-8ed41571e157][355]. The challenges and solutions for adopting DevSecOps are also identified [279].

**Software architecture and design patterns**, particularly microservices, receive considerable attention. Reviews analyze deployment and communication patterns in microservice architectures [14], testing approaches for microservice architecture-based applications [361], and security concerns within microservices [145][346]. The broader body of knowledge on microservice architecture is also summarized through tertiary studies [89]. Other architectural topics include architectural smells detection [237] and architecting for continuous deployment [117].

**Model-Driven Engineering (MDE)** is another recurring domain, with studies mapping its application in cyber-physical systems (CPS) [227][228], and for safety and security systems [219]. The use of recommender systems in MDE [30] and matching techniques [322] are also reviewed.

Notable results across these studies include the identification of a lack of common understanding in rapidly evolving areas like Continuous Experimentation [104], and the persistent challenge of managing technical debt, necessitating prioritization strategies [21]. The importance of analyzing app reviews for understanding user requirements [97] and the increasing problem of programming plagiarism in computing education [133] are also highlighted.

A common limitation observed across these mapping studies and reviews is the identification of **research gaps and underdeveloped areas**. For instance, despite the increasing number of aspect-oriented software development techniques, evidence of their real-world benefits remains scarce [271]. Similarly, the body of knowledge on Modern Code Review, while growing, is not yet fully understood as a whole [93]. The scarcity of research in Global Software Development (GSD) governance, despite its rising adoption, points to a significant gap [211]. Many studies conclude by calling for more empirical research, industry validation, or deeper investigation into specific sub-topics, indicating that while these reviews provide broad overviews, many areas still lack comprehensive solutions or empirical evidence.

The systematic mapping studies (SMS) and systematic literature reviews (SLR) presented here collectively delineate the research landscape across numerous software engineering domains, serving to synthesize existing knowledge, identify research gaps, and characterize the state of the art.

A substantial body of work focuses on **software quality and testing**. Reviews have comprehensively surveyed techniques for testing machine learning systems, addressing properties like correctness and robustness across various components [381]. The application of machine learning to automate software testing, driven by its complexity and cost, has been systematically mapped [96]. Further studies characterize model-based testing tools and challenges [356] and explore NLP-assisted software testing [120]. The concept of software testability has been surveyed, detailing numerous proposed techniques and metrics [121]. Specific areas like agile testing [109], test maturity assessment [122], and automation in mobile application testing [243] have also been reviewed. Software defect prediction is a recurring theme, with studies examining research landscapes [332], predictive analytics for defect severity [260], and the application of deep learning [131]. The impact of code smells on software bugs [71], software design smell detection [27], and the relationship between design patterns and bad smells [323] are also subjects of systematic inquiry.

**Requirements Engineering (RE)** is another prominent area. Studies have explored machine learning algorithms for identifying and classifying non-functional requirements [62] and RE activities within agile software development [92]. Specialized applications include RE for robotic systems [19][20], and eliciting requirements from app reviews using sentiment analysis [360]. The unique challenges of RE for Artificial Intelligence systems have also been mapped [4].

In **software architecture and design**, mapping studies have investigated customization solutions for Software as a Service (SaaS) applications [26], the evolution of SysML [364], and microservices architecture principles [115]. The decomposition of monoliths into microservices has been systematically reviewed [1], alongside an examination of microservice bad smells [367].

**Development methodologies and cross-cutting concerns** are frequently analyzed. Agile software development is a prominent area, with reviews on knowledge management strategies [263], challenges of using software size [141], and the use of metrics [186]. DevOps capabilities and practices have been explored through multivocal literature reviews [37], identifying challenges in continuous delivery [273]. Security is a critical concern, leading to reviews on threat analysis [342] and secure software development methodologies [179]. The role of Model-Driven Engineering (MDE) in software quality [134] and for Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) [229] has also been examined.

A notable pattern is the increasing focus on **emerging technologies and complex systems**. This includes systematic mappings on software engineering approaches for big data systems [fef977c8-e780-478d-ae09-766157113fe0], safety for mobile robotic systems [67], and self-adaptation in mobile apps [136]. The maintenance of Cyber-Physical Systems presents unique challenges due to their hardware-software combination [174]. Furthermore, the application of machine learning to IoT application testing is gaining traction [118].

Limitations inherent to these secondary studies often stem from their methodological scope. Many are systematic mapping studies, which prioritize breadth to identify research trends and gaps, rather than providing in-depth critical analysis of individual primary studies, as would be typical for a full systematic literature review. For instance, the systematic mapping on software performance research explicitly aims to clarify the state of research rather than delve deeply into specific solutions [144]. Similarly, the mapping of developer social network research identifies areas of use without necessarily evaluating the effectiveness of specific tools or methods [39]. A common finding across these studies is the identification of "unexplored" aspects or "gaps" in the literature [e.g., ba634d73-2d45-4154-9806-569d22c6e208, 158e3f05-2ad1-4c72-8d68-230a1b25fe84], indicating areas where further, more focused research is needed. The abstracts provided for some papers offer minimal detail on the methodology or key results of the *review itself*, making it challenging to fully assess their contributions and limitations without accessing the full text [e.g., d38dd7d3-3ce3-44fd-9797-d4696de657ac, 551c18dc-f180-4d21-8e8d-437b17cb8df9].

The landscape of software engineering research, as illuminated by recent systematic mapping studies and literature reviews, reveals a dynamic field grappling with evolving methodologies, complex system architectures, and the pervasive integration of artificial intelligence. A significant focus lies on modern software development paradigms, with numerous studies examining agile methods. Research in this area explores effort estimation, noting persistent gaps in literature regarding accuracy [113], risk management strategies [119], and the application of gamification to enhance developer engagement [288]. The integration of agile approaches for business process improvement [304] and the challenges of scaling agile solutions in large enterprises are also prominent [151]. DevOps, another key methodology, is explored in the context of microservices architecture [362] and the management of non-functional requirements [142]. Low-code development's modeling aspects are also under review [70].

Requirements Engineering (RE) remains a critical area, with studies addressing quality requirements (QRs), their empirical investigation [261], and the challenges of managing them in agile and rapid development environments where they are often ill-defined [54]. The identification and measurement of Requirements Technical Debt are also recurring themes [d5b92260-1a12-4644-aad2-3e114aaef760][223]. The use of controlled vocabularies to improve specification quality [5] and the impact of Use Cases in real-world projects [162] are further areas of investigation.

Software quality and testing are extensively covered, encompassing self-adaptive testing [316], model transformation testing [339], and mutation testing for mobile applications, which still presents challenges due to event-driven GUIs and complex execution environments [317]. Test case selection and prioritization are critical for both general software [318] and cyber-physical systems [294]. Cloud testing [58] and cloud-based mobile application testing [47] are also gaining attention. Fault localization, particularly search-based approaches, is explored for its potential automation benefits [164].

Architectural concerns are addressed through studies on microservices identification from legacy applications [235] and API deprecation practices [65]. Model-driven engineering is examined for mobile robotic systems [75] and the challenges of cross-domain model consistency checking [338]. Software evolution is also a focus, with refactoring studies emphasizing behavior preservation [32] and refactoring-aware code review [87].

Software security and safety are paramount, with research on Android source code vulnerability detection [309], data preparation for software vulnerability prediction [90], and the security risks posed by third-party libraries in Android apps [378]. Mobile app privacy concerns are also systematically mapped [98]. The complexities of software security patch management are highlighted [95], as are the costs associated with secure software development [352]. In safety-critical domains, development methodologies for machine learning applications in automotive systems are surveyed [277], alongside the incremental development of safety cases [29].

The increasing role of AI and machine learning (ML) in software engineering is a notable pattern. Studies investigate bots in software development [226], sentiment analysis tools in SE [256][257], and the application of ML for requirements identification [6] and addressing RE issues [135]. The broader field of Software Engineering for AI-Based Systems is also surveyed [214], alongside the testing of ML programs [312]. However, a significant limitation identified in predictive software engineering is the sensitivity of ML outcomes to randomization in data sampling and learning procedures, posing threats to reproducibility [194]. Other cross-cutting themes include cognition in software engineering [107], the comprehensive role of logging [128], and the critical review of grey literature in SE, noting a limited understanding of its utilization [168]. The adoption of quality evaluation models for open source software remains limited in practice despite their variety [375].

The field of software engineering extensively leverages systematic literature reviews (SLRs) and systematic mapping studies (SMS) to synthesize existing knowledge, identify research gaps, and chart future directions. A significant body of work, predominantly published between 2018 and 2019, demonstrates this trend, covering diverse sub-domains within software engineering. These reviews often aim to provide a comprehensive overview of a specific topic, offering classifications, frameworks, and empirical insights.

A prominent area of investigation is software testing and defect prediction. Studies have systematically analyzed cross-project defect prediction (CPDP) to understand the state-of-the-art in metrics, models, and data approaches [153]. Similarly, early software defect prediction has been mapped and reviewed, noting a limited focus on prior phases of the software development lifecycle [264]. The landscape of regression testing research has been explored to identify industry-relevant contributions [d7943093-8274-498b-96bd-c0d8fa3a8684], while the benefits and drawbacks of various software testing process models have been systematically reviewed [c1244b1d-8cca-4e68-a90c-f1f9bc74ffc2]. Furthermore, specialized areas like testing embedded software [123] and NLP-assisted software testing have been mapped to reduce manual effort in test case extraction [124].

Software architecture and modeling also represent a substantial focus. Reviews have classified multi-view approaches for software and system modeling [84] and provided a classification framework and research map for collaborative Model-Driven Software Engineering (MDSE) [116]. The execution of UML models has been systematically reviewed to identify and evaluate existing solutions [85]. Specific architectural concerns have been addressed through mapping studies on software architectures for context-aware systems [287] and robotic systems [8], both aiming to classify solutions and identify research progress.

Agile development practices and related challenges form another significant cluster. Systematic reviews have investigated the impact of time pressure on software quality and productivity [181] and analyzed communication channels and practices in Agile Software Development [7]. Mapping studies have explored the integration of agile methods with safety-critical systems [170] and the challenges of incorporating security into agile requirements engineering [357].

Software product lines (SPLs) and software reuse are also recurring themes. Studies have reviewed metrics for analyzing variability and its implementation in SPLs [101] and mapped the application of search-based software engineering to SPL problems [203]. The transfer of software reuse benefits to the industry has been systematically mapped, noting the long-standing interest in this area since 1968 [163].

Furthermore, the unique context of software startups has been examined through mapping studies focusing on software startup engineering [57] and the relevant software engineering knowledge areas [175]. Other reviews have investigated the detection and evolution of "smells" in object-oriented and service-oriented systems [292] and provided a systematic mapping of adaptive monitoring techniques across various domains [5100eab1-24d8-4724-aefc-b3be74127313].

A notable pattern across these papers is the consistent identification of research gaps and areas requiring further empirical evidence. For instance, the sporadic adoption of testing process models highlights a need for more evidence [c1244b1d-8cca-4e68-a90c-f1f9bc74ffc2]. Similarly, the limited focus on early phases in defect prediction [264] and the challenges in integrating security into agile requirements engineering [357] point to specific areas for future work. Many studies also contribute by proposing new classifications or frameworks to organize complex bodies of knowledge, such as for multi-view modeling [84] and collaborative MDSE [116]. While these reviews provide valuable syntheses, a common limitation, often implicit in their scope, is the inherent reliance on published literature, which may not fully capture industry practices or unpublished findings. The focus on specific sub-domains, while necessary for depth, also means that broader interdisciplinary connections might not be fully explored within individual reviews.

---

## 7. Discussion

### Research Gaps

Despite the growing interest and application of AI/ML in literature review methodologies, our comprehensive analysis of 1000 papers reveals several significant research gaps that warrant further investigation:

1.  **Holistic Automation Frameworks**: While numerous studies explore AI/ML applications for specific stages of systematic reviews (e.g., screening, data extraction), there is a notable absence of integrated, end-to-end AI/ML-driven frameworks capable of automating the *entire* systematic review process, from protocol development and search strategy refinement to data synthesis and reporting.
2.  **Rigorous Evaluation of AI/ML Tools**: The literature lacks standardized, comparative, and longitudinal studies rigorously evaluating the efficacy, reliability, and potential biases of AI/ML tools across diverse review contexts and domains (e.g., security vs. general software engineering). Most evaluations are ad-hoc and limited in scope, hindering generalizability and trust.
3.  **Ethical and Transparency Considerations**: The ethical implications of employing AI/ML in literature reviews, such as algorithmic bias in paper selection, data extraction, or synthesis, and the transparency of AI/ML decision-making processes, remain largely underexplored. This is particularly critical in sensitive domains like security where misinterpretations can have significant consequences.
4.  **Cross-Methodology Applicability**: The application and adaptation of AI/ML techniques specifically for different systematic review methodologies (e.g., mapping studies vs. traditional SLRs vs. rapid reviews) and their comparative performance are not thoroughly investigated. Most research tends to focus on traditional SLR workflows, leaving other valuable review types less supported by automation.
5.  **Human-AI Teaming and Workflow Integration**: There is limited research on optimal human-AI collaboration models and seamless integration of AI/ML tools into existing systematic review workflows. Understanding how human expertise can best complement AI capabilities to enhance both efficiency and rigor, rather than simply replacing manual tasks, is an underdeveloped area.

### Synthesis of Key Findings

The comprehensive review of 1000 papers reveals a dynamic landscape in systematic literature review methodology, increasingly influenced by the imperative for automation. A significant portion of the literature (223 papers) directly explores the application of AI/ML techniques to various stages of software engineering reviews, primarily focusing on automating paper screening, classification, and initial data extraction. This trend underscores a collective effort to address the scalability challenges posed by the exponential growth of academic publications.

Concurrently, the substantial bodies of work dedicated to "Systematic Reviews of AI/ML in Software" (169 papers) and "Systematic Reviews of Security Topics" (266 papers) highlight domains where the volume and criticality of research necessitate efficient and robust review methodologies. These areas, characterized by rapid evolution and high stakes, present fertile ground for the deployment and refinement of automated review techniques. The findings suggest that while AI/ML is being explored to manage the sheer volume of literature in these fields, the specific adaptations and evaluations for domain-specific nuances (e.g., technical jargon in security, rapid concept evolution in AI/ML) are still evolving.

Furthermore, the prominence of "Systematic Mapping Studies in Software Engineering" (342 papers) indicates a strong reliance on broad, exploratory reviews to map research landscapes. AI/ML holds immense potential here for initial topic identification, clustering, and trend analysis, significantly reducing the manual effort required for comprehensive overviews. Across all themes, a common thread is the pursuit of enhanced efficiency and, to a lesser extent, improved rigor and reproducibility in literature synthesis. While the adoption of AI/ML is evident, the current state suggests a fragmented approach, with many tools and techniques addressing specific sub-tasks rather than offering holistic, end-to-end automation solutions. The collective findings point towards an ongoing transition from purely manual review processes to increasingly human-AI collaborative paradigms, driven by the need to manage information overload while maintaining methodological soundness and addressing the inherent complexities of diverse research domains.

## 8. Conclusion

This systematic literature review, encompassing 1000 papers across key themes in automated literature review methodology, provides a comprehensive synthesis of the current state, emerging trends, and critical gaps in the field. Our primary contribution lies in delineating the increasing integration of AI/ML techniques into systematic review processes, particularly for tasks such as paper screening and classification, and highlighting their application across diverse domains like AI/ML in software and security. By synthesizing findings from systematic mapping studies and specific AI/ML applications, this review offers a structured understanding of how automation is reshaping the landscape of evidence synthesis in software engineering.

For practitioners, the findings underscore the potential of AI/ML to significantly enhance the efficiency and scalability of systematic reviews, enabling them to manage the ever-growing volume of academic literature more effectively. However, it also emphasizes the current fragmented nature of automation and the continued necessity for expert human oversight to ensure methodological rigor and mitigate potential biases. Practitioners are encouraged to explore existing AI/ML-assisted tools for specific review stages while remaining critical of their limitations.

For researchers, this review identifies pressing research gaps, particularly concerning the development of holistic automation frameworks, rigorous evaluation of AI/ML tools, and the exploration of ethical considerations in automated evidence synthesis. Future research should focus on creating integrated, end-to-end AI/ML platforms for systematic reviews, developing standardized metrics for evaluating their performance and reliability, and investigating optimal human-AI collaboration models. Furthermore, addressing algorithmic bias and extending automation capabilities to more complex analytical and synthesis tasks represent crucial avenues for advancing the field towards truly robust and trustworthy automated literature review methodologies.
